w:r.w:t: Revenue grew to $41,000 this month, up from $38,500 last month. That's a $2,500 lift, or 6.5% growth. Net income was $10,000, which is a 24.4% net margin. On the surface, both are good numbers.
But you said you added 2 stylists and your profit didn't go up the way you expected. You're right. Let's walk through why.

When you add 2 stylists on commission, every dollar they bring in costs you 45 to 50 cents in commission, plus product, plus a small share of fixed costs. So a $2,500 revenue lift turns into roughly $1,200 to $1,400 of marginal contribution before you cover any of their indirect cost. That's why the topline grew but the profit needle barely moved.

Your payroll ratio this month is 45.1%, which is high for a salon and tells us the new stylists are commission heavy and not yet booked solid. The single most useful thing you can do this month is set a clear weekly revenue target for each new chair and track utilization. The full recommendation is at the end of this report.
Revenue this month: $41,000. Prior month: $38,500. Change: $2,500, or 6.5%.
That's a solid lift, especially with 2 new stylists ramping. The question isn't whether revenue grew, it's whether it grew enough to justify the cost of adding 2 chairs.
The math you actually care about

Revenue per stylist before new hires: $38,500 divided by 7 equals $5,500 per stylist. Revenue per stylist after new hires: $41,000 divided by 9 equals $4,556 per stylist. Even though the topline grew, the per chair productivity dropped.

That's expected when ramping new stylists. They're booked 30 to 50% in their first 60 days while they build a book. The question is whether they'll get to 70 to 85% utilization within 90 days. If they don't, the math doesn't work.
The 2 new stylists are likely contributing about $1,200 to $1,400 a month in profit between them right now
They need to ramp to roughly $4,500 to $5,500 each in monthly billings to be net positive on a fully loaded basis (commission, benefits, product, share of fixed cost)
That target is reachable, but only if you actively manage their book building. It rarely happens on its own
Here's where every dollar of revenue went this month, with industry benchmarks for an owner operated salon.

Payroll at 45.1% is at the high end. With 9 stylists that's $2,055 of payroll per stylist on average, which lines up with a commission heavy structure. If you raised commission rates recently or shifted toward more contractor splits, that's why this number is creeping

Net margin of 24.4% is strong for a salon. The new stylist economics aren't broken, but they aren't optimal either. A typical mature stylist contributes 8 to 12% to net margin once fully booked. Yours are contributing closer to 3 to 4% right now
Estimated leak: $1,500 to $2,500 per month in foregone profit.

If your 2 new stylists are at 40% utilization and your goal is 75%, you're leaving roughly 35% of their chair time empty. At an average ticket of $85 and 3 services per hour, that's $250 an hour in unbooked revenue per stylist. Even at 50% margin contribution, that's serious money once you add it up across the month.

$4,800 in product is fine if half of that is being resold to clients at retail margin. If most of it is back bar (used in services with no retail markup), you're absorbing the full cost. Salons that hit 15% retail revenue per ticket make 35 to 45% margin on that piece. If your retail mix is under 5%, you're leaving real money on the table.

3.4% in misc is hiding several recurring charges. Common in salons: software (booking app, POS, email marketing), credit card processing, towel service, music licensing, and small equipment. Once you split this out, the conversation becomes "do I still need all of these?" and the answer is usually no for at least one of them.
4. Rent slightly high for revenue level
Estimated leak: not immediate, but a flag.

Rent at 10.2% of revenue is at the upper end of where salons can comfortably operate. If revenue grows 15% from here, rent drops to a healthy 8.9% naturally. If revenue stalls, rent becomes a real constraint. Worth knowing where you stand on the lease and whether a renewal is coming up in the next 12 months.
$1,200 in marketing is in range, but if you can't tell me which dollar is bringing in new clients versus filling existing stylist books, you can't optimize it. Most salons get 60% of new clients
from one channel and don't know which one. Setting up a one question intake ("how did you find us?") closes that gap immediately.
Salons usually have cleaner cash flow than restaurants or contractors because most clients pay at the time of service. The cash issue here isn't timing, it's allocation.
Net income this month: $10,000. That's about $333 a day in cash building. Should be visible in your bank balance growing $2,000 to $2,500 a week before owner draws.
Owner draws not separated from operating cash. Easy to underestimate how much you're actually pulling out when it comes from one account
Inventory build on retail product. If you stocked up on product to support the 2 new stylists, that's $1,500 to $3,000 sitting on shelves
Tax savings not earmarked. At a 24.4% margin, you'll owe meaningful self employment and income tax. If it isn't sitting in a separate account, you'll feel it in April
New stylists ramp slowly on their own. Revenue lifts to $42,000 to $43,000 within 90 days. Profit creeps up modestly.

Set weekly revenue targets for new stylists. Owner manages their book building actively (referral bonuses, social media features, walk in priority). Both new stylists hit 70% utilization by day 60. Adds $4,000 a month.
Same as above, plus a retail attach program that pushes retail revenue from current level to 12 to 15% of every ticket. Adds another $1,500 to $2,000 a month at 40% margin.
Set a weekly revenue target for each new stylist and track actual versus target every Sunday.

Target: $1,100 in week 1, $1,400 in week 4, $1,800 in week 8, $2,200 by week 12. That gets each stylist to roughly $9,000 a month at full ramp. Every Sunday, sit down for 10 minutes with each new stylist. Look at last week's number versus target. If they're behind, what's the plan this week. If they're ahead, what's working that we can scale.

This is the answer to the question you actually asked. You added 2 chairs and didn't see the profit go up. The reason is they aren't booked yet. Adding chairs doesn't make money. Filling chairs makes money. Most salon owners assume new stylists will book themselves up. They don't. Active management cuts ramp time roughly in half.
Print a one page tracker for each stylist: weeks 1 through 12, target for each week, actual revenue, gap
Have a 10 minute Sunday check in. Target versus actual, what's working, what's blocking
If a stylist falls 20% behind target two weeks in a row, do something different: pair them with your busiest stylist for a week, feature them on social, give them walk in priority for 2 weeks
If a stylist hits target two weeks in a row, raise the target by 10%

If both new stylists hit their week 12 target of $2,200 a week ($9,500 a month each), you add $19,000 a month in revenue from current $4,500 each. At 50% commission and small fixed cost share, that's $7,000 a month in additional net income, or $84,000 a year.
This week: print the 12 week ramp tracker for each new stylist. Have the first Sunday meeting
This week: split the misc bucket. Look for one recurring charge to cancel
This month: install a one question intake at the front desk: "how did you find us?"
Next 60 days: design and roll out a retail attach program. Goal is to push retail revenue from current level to 12% of each ticket
These four steps move you from "hoping the new stylists work out" to "managing them actively to a number." That's the difference between a 24% margin business and a 32% margin business.
Questions on any of this? Reply to the email this came with. Next month's report will track stylist ramp progress, retail mix, and overall margin.
